concurrent-control.short: A comparison group living through the same period.
concurrent-control.text: Compare against a group measured over the same period, so trends and regression to the mean hit both equally.

parallel-trends.name: Pre-trend check & control series
parallel-trends.short: Show the groups moved together before the change.
parallel-trends.text: Show the groups moved in parallel before the intervention, or add a comparison series it couldn't have affected.

cluster-allocation.name: Allocate by cluster
cluster-allocation.short: Assign whole groups, so nothing leaks between arms.
cluster-allocation.text: Assign whole groups (classes, wards, villages) so the intervention can't leak into the control group.

washout.name: Washout period
washout.short: Let the first treatment wear off.
washout.text: Leave enough time between treatment periods for the previous effect to disappear.

external-validation.name: External validation
external-validation.short: Test it on data it has never seen.
external-validation.text: Test the model or method on data from another time or place that it has never seen.

multiplicity.name: Multiplicity correction
multiplicity.short: Name one primary outcome, or pay for every extra test.
multiplicity.text: Name one primary outcome, or adjust for the number of tests you run.

replication.name: Independent replication
replication.text: Another team, sample or site repeats the study, ideally with the same pre-registered plan.

comprehensive-search.name: Comprehensive search
comprehensive-search.text: Search multiple databases, trial registries, preprints and grey literature, and contact authors.

grey-appraisal.name: Grey-literature appraisal
grey-appraisal.short: Grade every grey source before you trust it.
grey-appraisal.text: Score each grey source for its producer's authority, stated method, objectivity, date and outlet tier, and set stopping rules for the search in advance.

heterogeneity-plan.name: Pre-planned heterogeneity analysis
heterogeneity-plan.short: Plan in advance how you'll explain why studies differ.
heterogeneity-plan.text: Random-effects models plus pre-specified subgroups and meta-regression to explore why studies differ.

sampling-frame.name: Representative sampling
sampling-frame.short: Sample from the whole population, not the convenient part.
sampling-frame.text: Recruit from a defined population (all consecutive patients, a random sample), not whoever is convenient.

validated-measures.name: Validated, objective measures
validated-measures.short: Use instruments proven to measure what matters.
validated-measures.text: Use calibrated instruments, records or validated scales instead of memory or ad-hoc questions, and outcomes that matter rather than unvalidated surrogates.

reflexivity.name: Reflexivity & double coding
reflexivity.short: Write down your own lens, and let a second coder check.
reflexivity.text: Keep an audit trail and reflexive notes, have a second analyst code independently, check interpretations with participants.

triangulation.name: Triangulation
triangulation.short: Different methods, different flaws, same answer.
triangulation.text: Combine sources, methods or designs with different weaknesses. Trust the conclusions they agree on.

saturation-sampling.name: Theoretical sampling to saturation
saturation-sampling.short: Keep sampling until nothing new turns up.
saturation-sampling.text: Keep adding cases chosen to challenge emerging ideas, until new data add nothing new.

multilevel-analysis.name: Multilevel analysis
multilevel-analysis.short: Model people inside groups inside places.
multilevel-analysis.text: Model individuals nested in groups, using individual-level data wherever possible.

verification-validation.name: Verification & validation
verification-validation.short: Check the code is right, then check the model matches reality.
verification-validation.text: Verify that the code solves the equations correctly (convergence tests, unit checks); validate the model against real experiments.

multi-site.name: Multi-site, diverse sample
multi-site.short: Run it where the results will be used.
multi-site.text: Run the study across the settings and populations where the results will actually be used.

within-comparison.name: Self or sibling comparison
within-comparison.short: Compare people with themselves, or siblings with siblings.
within-comparison.text: Compare units with themselves, or siblings with each other, so stable background factors cancel out.

spc.name: Run charts & control limits
spc.short: Judge a change against the process's own baseline variation.
spc.text: Plot the measure over time from a stable baseline and apply pre-set rules (shifts, trends, control limits), so real change stands out from noise and drift.

T01.name: The ethics board says no
T01.text: Withholding or assigning the exposure is judged unethical. No one may be allocated to it.

T02.name: Funding cut
T02.text: You now have six months and a tenth of the budget.

T03.name: Rarer than you thought
T03.text: New data: the outcome affects about 1 in 20,000, not 1 in 200.

T04.name: The registry door opens
T04.text: A national registry with 20 years of linked records becomes available to you.

T05.name: The ministry sets a threshold
T05.text: Eligibility will be decided by a score: everyone above 60 gets it, everyone below doesn't.

T06.name: It's happening anyway
T06.text: The decision is made: everyone gets the intervention within a year. Only the order is open.

T07.name: They talk to each other
T07.text: Participants share tips, materials and gossip. Anything you give one of them, the others get too.

T08.name: Only one
T08.text: It turns out there is only one eligible unit: one patient, one plant, one country.

T09.name: Thirty studies just dropped
T09.text: A literature search reveals dozens of primary studies on this exact question.

T10.name: Into the fog
T10.text: Experts can't agree what the key variables even are.

T11.name: Slow burn
T11.text: The effect, if any, would take 15 years to show.

T12.name: A brief trigger
T12.text: The suspected cause lasts minutes, and the effect comes within hours.

T13.name: Only a few are exposed
T13.text: The exposure is confined to a few hundred people at one site.

T14.name: Reviewer 2
T14.text: The Reviewer may play one extra Threat against every method this round.

T15.name: Replication crisis
T15.text: Any method not defended with Preregistration or Independent replication loses 1 point this round.

T16.name: Open science prize
T16.text: +1 point to every player who plays Preregistration, Triangulation or Independent replication this round.

T17.name: It's all on the blogs
T17.text: The journals turn up five papers. The practitioners have written five hundred posts, talks and white papers.

P1.name: Screens & teen mental health
P1.brief: Is social media harming adolescents' mental health? Parents, platforms and governments want an answer.
stages: How do teenagers themselves describe their social-media use and its effects?
How common are heavy use and depressive symptoms, and do they co-occur?
Does heavy use come before rising symptoms, or the other way round?
Does cutting use for four weeks improve mood?
What do all the trials and cohorts add up to?

P2.name: Microplastics in our bodies
P2.brief: Microplastics turn up in blood, placentas and arteries. Are they a health problem?
stages: What has been studied so far, with which methods, and where are the gaps?
Do different labs measuring the same tissue sample find the same particle counts?
How much do people carry, and does it vary by region and age?
Do people with more microplastics in arterial plaque have more heart attacks later?
Through what cellular mechanism could particles cause inflammation, and at what dose?

P3.name: A soft gripper for fruit picking
P3.brief: Growers can't find seasonal workers. Can a soft robotic gripper pick strawberries without bruising them?
stages: What gripper designs exist, and how have they been evaluated?
Design a gripper that growers and pickers find usable.
Which combination of finger material, pressure and approach speed minimizes bruising?
Does it beat existing grippers on a shared set of fruits and metrics?
Can it run a full shift in a real greenhouse? Will staff keep using it?

P4.name: The four-day week
P4.brief: A government wants to know if a 32-hour week at full pay is good for workers and firms.
stages: How did the first companies that tried it make it work, or fail?
Can firms be recruited, and can productivity and well-being be measured consistently?
Sixty firms volunteered and all will switch eventually. Does it affect burnout and output?
A whole country adopted it by law in one year. What happened to national productivity?
Why does it work in some sectors and not in others?

P5.name: A new post-viral syndrome
P5.brief: Months after a new infection, some people report exhaustion and brain fog. What is it, and what helps?
stages: What do the first patients look like?
How common is it among people who were infected?
Who is at risk? Does vaccination before infection change the odds?
Twelve candidate treatments are proposed. Which work?
Ranking the treatments when few were compared head-to-head.

P6.name: AI triage in the emergency department
P6.brief: A hospital group wants an AI tool that flags patients who will need intensive care.
stages: Can routine data predict ICU admission within 24 hours?
Does it still work at another hospital, a year later?
Do nurses agree with each other, and with the tool, on the triage level?
The tool will be switched on in all 8 hospitals this year. Does it save lives?
Why do some clinicians override it so often?
